title: Targeting cellular adaptive responses to glutaminolysis perturbation for cancer therapy

sections.abstract:
Metabolic aberrations, notably deviations in glutamine metabolism, are crucial in the oncogenic process, offering vital resources for the unlimited proliferation and enhanced survival capabilities of cancer cells. The dependency of malignant cells on glutamine metabolism has led to the proposition of targeted therapeutic strategies. However, the capability of cancer cells to initiate adaptive responses undermines the efficacy of these therapeutic interventions. This review meticulously examines the multifaceted adaptive mechanisms that cancer cells deploy to sustain survival and growth following the disruption of glutamine metabolism. Emphasis is placed on the roles of transcription factors, alterations in metabolic pathways, the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 signaling axis, autophagy, macropinocytosis, nucleotide biosynthesis, and the scavenging of ROS. Thus, the delineation and subsequent targeting of these adaptive responses in the context of therapies aimed at glutamine metabolism offer a promising avenue for circumventing drug resistance in cancer treatment.

Keywords: Adaptive response, Cancer therapy, Glutamine metabolism
sections.introduction:
Metabolic abnormalities serve as hallmarks of many cancer cells, defining dysregulation or reprogramming of metabolism ( Tennant et al., 2010 ). These significant deviations in cancer cell metabolism, compared to normal cells, equip them with the ability to sustain unlimited proliferation and gain survival advantages ( Zhu and Thompson, 2019 ). An increased demand for glutamine, the most abundant amino acid in the body, is one of the metabolic dependencies propelling cancer progression ( Wise and Thompson, 2010 ). Glutaminolysis is a metabolic process in which cells utilize glutamine to generate energy, maintain redox homeostasis, and produce essential molecules, including amino acids and nucleotides, necessary for the unrestricted growth of cancer ( Wise and Thompson, 2010 , Yoo et al., 2020 ). Glutaminase (GLS), which is the first and rate-limiting enzyme in mitochondrial glutamine metabolism, catabolizes glutamine into glutamate. Glutamate is further converted into α-ketoglutarate, an intermediate of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, via glutamate dehydrogenase 1 or transaminases, such as glutamate-oxaloacetate transaminase 2 (GOT2) or glutamate-pyruvate transaminase 2 (GPT2) ( Fig. 1 ). This glutamine metabolism is crucial for introducing carbon into the TCA cycle, which is known as mitochondrial anaplerosis and contributes to the predominant production of ammonia within cells ( Jones and Thompson, 2009 , Yoo et al., 2020 ).

Glutamine metabolism and targets for cancer treatment. The catabolic process of glutamine is initiated with its transport into cells through membrane-bound glutamine transporters, such as solute carrier family 1 member 5 (SLC1A5). A specific variant of SLC1A5 serving as a mitochondrial glutamine transporter, facilitates the transport of cytoplasmic glutamine into the mitochondria matrix. Inside the mitochondria, glutamine is converted into glutamate by GLS, marking the first key enzyme for mitochondrial glutamine catabolism. Subsequently, glutamate undergoes transformation into α-ketoglutarate by either GLUD1 or GOT2/GPT2 enzymes. This conversion supports the TCA cycle. The inhibitors targeting these pivotal steps in glutamine metabolism, highlighted in red, represent potential therapeutic strategies in cancer treatment. GLUD1, glutamate dehydrogenase 1.

Given the metabolic reliance of cancer cells on glutamine metabolism, it has prompted the development of therapeutic strategies targeting this pathway in the pursuit of effective cancer treatment ( Yang et al., 2021 ). Specifically, antagonists for glutamine and inhibitors targeting enzymes involved in glutamine metabolic pathways have been developed ( Fig. 1 ). These compounds have undergone rigorous evaluation to ascertain their therapeutic efficacy in cancer treatments, as detailed in Table 1 . Nevertheless, cumulative evidence indicates that several drugs targeting glutamine metabolism exhibit a limited tumor-suppressive effect ( Altman et al., 2016 ). As cancer cells retain the ability to adapt to metabolic challenges, these adaptive responses enable them to survive and proliferate even in conditions of restricted glutamine metabolism through the rewiring or remodeling of their metabolic pathways ( Kim et al., 2019 , Kim et al., 2023 ). Therefore, comprehending these compensatory mechanisms is imperative for the development of more effective therapeutic strategies targeting cancer cells ( Jin et al., 2023 ). This review provides an overview of the various adaptive responses of cancer cells to the perturbation in glutamine metabolism. Additionally, we explore opportunities for developing therapeutic approaches that target these metabolic adaptations.

sections.conclusion: In summary, this paper has offered a comprehensive overview of the complex adaptive responses of cancer cells to anticancer strategies that target glutamine metabolism. It underscores the urgent need for the development of innovative therapeutic approaches that aim at these alternative survival mechanisms. Continued research in this area is essential for advancing our knowledge of cancer metabolism, potentially heralding a new era in cancer treatment.
